title: A flagged gap in a group of three
context: SYNTHETIC SCENARIO (no real employee data). An automated pay-equity dashboard flags that, among Level-6 principal designers, the one woman earns 16% less than the average of the two men. That's the entire population at that level: three people. Leadership splits into two camps. One insists this is clear evidence of gender discrimination and wants an immediate correction. The other waves it off: 'Three people, one of each comparison — that's statistically meaningless, ignore it.' There is no regression to run and no larger cohort. The three have differing tenures, specializations, and last-promotion dates, none of which has yet been examined. The company wants a defensible, honest way to handle the flag.
question: How should the company handle this flag, and what is wrong with both camps' positions?
gold_notes: n=3 is far too small for any statistical inference — you can neither conclude discrimination nor conclude 'nothing here' from the number alone.
The right response to a tiny-sample flag is an individualized review of the three cases (tenure, specialization, promotion timing, performance, any bona fide factors), not a statistical verdict.
'It's clearly discrimination' overclaims from noise; 'it's statistically meaningless, ignore it' wrongly treats un-analyzed individual pay as automatically fine — both skip the actual work.
If the individualized review surfaces an unexplained gap, remediate it upward and document the reasoning; if legitimate factors fully explain it, document that instead.
Small samples call for case-by-case scrutiny and documentation, precisely because statistics can't adjudicate them.
trap: Drawing a conclusion from n=3 in either direction — declaring it proof of discrimination, or dismissing it as statistically meaningless and ignoring it — instead of doing the individualized, documented review a tiny sample actually requires.
